newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia mining giant fears copper price will fall.
newsitem.headline: Australia mining giant fears copper price will fall.

text.p: Australian mining giant MIM Holdings Ltd fears weak copper prices will continue to weigh on its bottom line just as it enters a period of growth and cooperation with its once-militant workforce.

"We have a huge capital programme ahead of us," the mining firm's chief executive, Nick Stump, told reporters after reporting an annual net profit of A$170.6 million (US$134.8 million) for the year ended June 30. In the previous year, the company suffered a A$216.1 million loss.
Stump said the company was forfeiting a bigger second-half dividend than the 1.25 cents declared to help fund the company's growth.

MIM was able to operate its main Mount Isa base metal and silver mine in central Queensland profitably in the 1995/1996 fiscal year after restoring production and lowering costs, although weaker copper prices depressed the bottom line.
The mine recently signed peace pacts with 2,500 Mount Isa workers, ensuring the bitter industrial disputes and lockouts that last year dragged the company into the red would not be repeated.
But despite the headway, by June Mount Isa had once again become a loss-making operation as world copper prices tumbled in the wake of the Sumitomo Corp trading scandal.
Stump said the company believes there was a chance copper prices could go up.
Unlike some other mining companies, MIM does not cover what it produces with hedge positions, a type of insurance mechanism, leaving its bottom line exposed to market prices.
Each 10 percent move in the copper price over the year is worth A$37 million to MIM's profits.
Uncertainties over the copper price come as MIM readies its huge Ernest Henry and Alumbrera mines for production and embarks on a A$500 million expansion of the Mount Isa lode.
Ernest Henry is being developed near Mount Isa with another Australian mining house, Savage Resources Ltd, to produce some 85,000 tonnes of copper annually.
The company is committed to spending A$500 million to extend the life of Mount Isa into the next century and is the lead partner in the A$1 billion Alumbrera mine of Argentina.
The project is the first of its kind in Argentina and is scheduled to begin producing some 180,000 tonnes of copper annually next year.
Analysts believe the main factor driving down the copper market is over-production.
While world copper supply is largely in line with current demand, expansion and new mines slated to come on stream soon mean the market is heading for a big surplus, they said.
